authors: Wilson, M.L., Boesch, C., Fruth, B., Furuichi, T., Gilby, I.C., Hashimoto, C., Hobaiter, C.L., Hohmann, G., Itoh, N., Koops, K., Lloyd, J.N., Matsuzawa, T., Mitani, J.C., Mjungu, D.C., Morgan, D., Muller, M.N., Mundry, R., Nakamura, M., Pruetz, J., Pusey, A.E., Riedel, J., Sanz, C., Schel, A.M., Simmons, N., Waller, M., Watts, D.P., White, F., Wittig, R.M., Zuberbuhler, K., Wrangham, R.W.
title: Lethal aggression in Pan is better explained by adaptive strategies than human impacts
data_extracted: 152 killings across 18 chimp + 4 bonobo communities; 92% attackers male; 73% victims male; median attacker-to-victim ratio 8:1; bonobos NOT observed to kill in any community

authors: Wrangham, R.W., Wilson, M.L., Muller, M.N.
title: Comparative rates of violence in chimpanzees and humans
data_extracted: Intercommunity killing rate (median across 5 populations): 69-287 deaths/100,000/year. Intragroup: 261-271 deaths/100,000/year. Total chimp violence mortality: 271 (271-287) deaths/100,000/year. Comparable to human subsistence-farmer warfare (median 595/100,000/yr). Non-lethal physical attack rate: chimp males 2,301 attacks/100,000h vs human adult Aboriginal Australian ~6/100,000h: ratio 182-384x.

title: Lethal coalitionary aggression associated with a community fission in chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) at Ngogo, Kibale National Park, Uganda
data_extracted: 2 confirmed + 1 suspected killings 2018-2019; victims Erroll (15.5y) and Basie (33y); attack coalitions 5-10+ males; Western community attackers; Central community victims; followed 2015 community fission

authors: Mouginot, M., Wilson, M.L., Desai, N., Surbeck, M.
title: Differences in expression of male aggression between wild bonobos and chimpanzees
data_extracted: Bonobo male-male aggression ~3x chimp male-male aggression rate; bonobos higher contact-aggression rate. Chimps more likely male-female aggression; bonobos almost exclusively male-male. Sites: Kokolopori (3 bonobo communities), Gombe (2 chimp communities). N=12 bonobos + 14 chimps focal followed. PUBLISHED FINDING: more-aggressive male bonobos achieve HIGHER mating success.

authors: Surbeck, M., Fruth, B., et al.
title: Drivers of female power in bonobos
data_extracted: 30 years demographic+behavioral data across 6 wild bonobo communities (Kokolopori, Wamba, LuiKotale sites). 85% of female coalitions targeted males. Kokolopori 2020: females dominated 98.4% of conflicts with males. Eyengo 1998: females never outranked by male. Female-female alliances form despite unrelated immigration (philopatry pattern: females disperse from natal group).

authors: Torfs, J.R.R., Stevens, J.M.G., Verspeek, J., Lameris, D.W., Guery, J.-P., Eens, M., Staes, N.
title: Multi-group analysis of grooming network position in a highly social primate
data_extracted: 22 captive bonobo groups; 84 unique individuals (51 female, 33 male); 136 datapoints; group size 3-15 (median 6); sex ratio M/F 0.20-2.00 (14 female-biased, 3 male-biased, 4 balanced); mean 626 scans/group, mean 316 grooming interactions/group. Mother-reared > atypically-reared in centrality. Group size effect on disparity beta=-0.025 (negative). Eigenvector centrality declined with group size: females beta=-0.030 (stronger), males beta=-0.007. NO significant sex-ratio effects detected on network position.

authors: Funkhouser, J.A., Mayhew, J.A., Mulcahy, J.B.
title: Social network and dominance hierarchy analyses at Chimpanzee Sanctuary Northwest
data_extracted: 7 sanctuary chimps (1 male, 6 female, ages 33-43y), 106.75 obs hours. Proximity strength 3.62-4.50 mean 4.12; eigenvector centrality 0.34-0.41 mean 0.38; clustering coefficient 0.66-0.73 mean 0.49. Grooming strength 593-3420 sec, mean 1808. Agonistic modularity Q=0.33. de Vries linearity h'=0.43 p=0.38 (non-linear in this small sanctuary group). Modified David's scores -8.58 to +5.71. ALLOGROOMING was NON-RECIPROCAL (p=0.95) in this captive chimp group; AGONISM was RECIPROCAL (Mantel Z p=0.049).

title: Egalitarian despots: hierarchy steepness, reciprocity and the grooming-trade model in wild chimpanzees, Pan troglodytes
data_extracted: Sonso/Budongo steepness=0.70 (8 males); M-group/Mahale 2011 steepness=0.30 (10 males). Other steepness values from same paper: M-group 1985=0.22, M-group 1992=0.57, Kanyawara 1998=0.39, North-group Tai 1993=0.39. Sonso grooming directed 60% UP-hierarchy; M-group 49%. Sonso grooming/rank rank-correlation rho=0.905 p=0.002; M-group rho=-0.030 ns. Sonso frequency-reciprocity 0.45 < M-group 0.66.

authors: Stevens, J.M.G., Vervaecke, H., De Vries, H., Van Elsacker, L.
title: Sex Differences in the Steepness of Dominance Hierarchies in Captive Bonobo Groups
data_extracted: 6 captive bonobo groups. Hierarchies HIGHLY LINEAR but males steeper than females. Female dominance INCOMPLETE - 'nonexclusive female dominance' (some males dominate some females). Specific numerical steepness values not confirmed without full-text.

authors: Krupenye, C., Tan, J., Hare, B.
title: Bonobos voluntarily hand food to others but not toys or tools
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
data_extracted: Bonobos directly transfer FOOD (nuts) significantly more in test than control (p<0.001 both models). Bonobos do NOT transfer rocks/tools. 10 dyads of 2 bonobos (2M:10F, ages 5-15y). Sharing UNSOLICITED (no gesture effect; no rank effect; no reciprocity effect). Bonobos cracked palm nuts at 2.8 nuts/min median. Asymmetric finding: bonobos share food NOT tools; chimps share tools NOT food.

authors: Nolte, S., Sterck, E.H.M., van Leeuwen, E.J.C.
title: Does tolerance allow bonobos to outperform chimpanzees on a cooperative task? A conceptual replication of Hare et al., 2007
data_extracted: 9 bonobos vs 16 chimps co-feeding; 7 bonobos vs 11 chimps cooperation. CO-FEEDING SIMILAR between species (chi-sq=0.39, p=0.533) - REPLICATION REJECTED tolerance-difference. COOPERATION on monopolizable food: bonobos > chimps (t=2.51, p=0.017; chi-sq=5.08, p=0.024). Co-feeding aggression: chimps HIGHER (t=-3.02, p=0.002). Socio-sexual contact during cooperation: bonobos HIGHER (t=2.75, p=0.012).

title: Female contributions to the peaceful nature of bonobo society
data_extracted: Adult sex ratio bonobos at Wamba ~0.75 male/female (near 1:1). Females take initiative in ranging. No confirmed bonobo infanticide. Bonobo females form close associations; chimp females do not.

authors: Tokuyama, N., Sakamaki, T., Furuichi, T.
title: Inter-group aggressive interaction patterns indicate male mate defense and female cooperation across bonobo groups at Wamba, Democratic Republic of the Congo
data_extracted: 3 neighboring bonobo groups at Wamba. KEY FINDING: female cross-group cooperation. Aggression female-vs-female between groups RARE. Females sometimes form COALITIONS WITH OUT-GROUP individuals to attack common target. Male intergroup aggression = mate defense (within-group orientation); female intergroup interaction = tolerance + cross-group cooperation.

title: The evolutionary roots of lethal conflict (News & Views on Wilson 2014)
data_extracted: Confirms 152 killings in 18 chimp + 4 bonobo communities. Bonobos NOT observed to kill regardless of human-impact level. Lethal coalitionary attacks on neighboring-community individuals documented ONLY in chimpanzees among great apes.
